description: Stanford CS/physics student building a cited, physics-checked dashboard over NASA PSI microgravity combustion data for Flame in Freefall.
summary:
Matching oxygen partial pressure does not necessarily reproduce the same combustion behavior. FlameMap connects NASA PSI tables, published fire experiments and cited AI summaries so habitat researchers can compare relevant evidence and identify what still needs testing.

A researcher planning a fabric-fire study for a pressurized lunar rover enters 30% O2 and 70.3 kPa. FlameMap shows that none of the 263 solid-material tests in the 20 loaded PSI tables comes within 7.8 O2 points of that level (the highest is 22.2%, BASS-II) and that none of them reports pressure. It then points to NASA reports in which Saffire V and VI burned cotton, SIBAL fabric and PMMA in orbit at 26–31% O2, shows each cited AI summary beside its source excerpts, and exports the matching rows with every original cell.

Where the tables do reach that oxygen level, behavior differed at a similar O2 partial pressure: FLEX droplet burning-rate constants were 1.18–1.27× higher at 30% O2 and 0.7 atm than in air at 1 atm, and more ACME CFI-G gas flames kept burning at 34–40% O2. Every number traces to a PSI row, a report table or a stated formula.
details:
What it does.

• Evidence views distinguish ambient oxygen from burner oxidizer oxygen, show solid materials without inventing pressure, and expose native variables for experiments that do not fit an atmosphere map. Coverage counts use individual tests and the selected fuel class. FLEX-2 range summaries are context, not measured combinations. The inventory and inspector retain all rows.

• Scenario comparisons use reported oxygen, pressure and flow plus fuel and optional material. Missing requested dimensions prevent a complete score. Lunar, Martian and terrestrial targets are explicitly unsupported by the microgravity condition ranking. Oxygen-gap statements scan all matching tests, independently of which row is first in a collection.

• Investigation cards show row-cited ranges, changing and constant source columns, documented conditions and exact source excerpts. Saffire and SPICE retrieval includes result documents.

• The PSI catalog shows all 24 Combustion Science records with PSI's objectives, hardware and Earth-benefit text. Twenty loaded tables cover 18 of these investigations.

• Gravity comparisons place the reported Saffire-II microgravity and 1-g burns side by side. They are measurements at those conditions, not lunar/Martian predictions or mathematical bounds.

• Earth applications show verbatim NASA passages about water mist, smoke detection and firefighter equipment, linked to their source pages.

• The public question box retrieves evidence for arbitrary questions. Scenario changes recompute explanations without a server, API key or paid model call.

• CSV export includes every original cell, normalized values and provenance, ignition outcomes and available final O2/CO2/CO measurements. Missing outcome labels remain missing; conditions-only tables are identified before users consider training a predictive model.

How it works. Twelve original tables stay byte-exact in raw_psi/; eight added tables are stored with a separate manifest in derived/sources/. Hash checks precede normalization. Values retain PSI ID, filename, CSV row, source cell and source unit. Ambient oxygen and burner oxidizer oxygen remain separate. Units are normalized only when their interpretation is supported.

Physics checks cover declared units and ranges, complete ambient-mixture sums, ignition/burn-time consistency, droplet-diameter consistency and reported final gas fractions. Zero burn time with Hot ignition = No is a valid non-ignition outcome. The d² diagnostic applies only to rows with the required droplet measurements and does not become a solid-fire prediction.

The source engine uses deterministic BM25 retrieval. Exact excerpts retain their original document and page citations. Generated answers are rechecked on every read: exact excerpts are shown as quotes; a paraphrase is shown, labelled, only when its citations are verbatim, its numbers and units follow the cited excerpt in order, no direction or negation word contradicts the excerpt, and it is approved in a recorded review list (75 approved, 3 rejected; review performed with an SI coding assistant). Fabricated quotations, uncited claims, swapped values and reversed wording are withheld. Automated checks verify citation text and number–unit consistency; scientific meaning requires review. Scenario scores average only measured conditions; fuel and material are gates, and a "close" test must lie within 5 O2 points and a 1.5× pressure ratio. Numeric checks and a human review sample are generated under derived/verification/.

Findings from the tables. CFI-G and FLEX are the only loaded tables with per-test outcomes suited to statistical tests (Saffire-II has nine textual burn outcomes; BASS-II and Flame Design hold end-state gas readings, not flammability labels). We used threshold grid searches with test-day-grouped cross-validation and permutation tests, least squares with bootstrap intervals and matched condition cells (method, scripts and limits in notes/findings.md and notes/analysis/). The automated tests and value re-derivation establish reproducibility, not causal interpretation.

• Similar O2 partial pressure, different droplet burning rates (FLEX). The d²-law burning-rate constant at 30% O2 and 0.7 atm (21.5 kPa O2) was 1.27× the air value at 1 atm (21.4 kPa) for methanol (exploratory 95% CI 1.16–1.42; FLEX tests 25, 26, 40, 41) and 1.18× for heptane (1.03–1.36; tests 27, 28, 42, 43). The eight elevated-O2 tests come from two test days and the interval resamples tests, not days. None of them ended in flame extinction (7 droplet disruptions, 1 completion) against 14 of 29 air tests, but disruption ends a test before extinction could be observed, and the FLEX report discusses fuel-needle contamination. The air burning-rate comparison uses 27 tests because 2 lack a reported constant. In nitrogen-diluted tests at 0.70–1.02 atm, a model in which only O2 partial pressure matters is rejected: the log-coefficients for O2 fraction and total pressure differ (methanol 0.35 vs 0.01, heptane 0.44 vs 0.08; day-clustered 95% intervals of the difference 0.23–0.49 and 0.18–0.59). This is consistent with NASA's 1-g finding that material flammability depends more on O2 concentration than on equivalent partial pressure (NTRS 20160001047); it is not a validation of any droplet model.

• More CFI-G gas flames kept burning at elevated O2. Of hot-ignited normal flames, 41 of 41 at 18–23% O2 self-extinguished, while 28 of 89 at 34–40% O2 were still burning when the fuel flow was stopped (right-censored: when they would have extinguished is unknown), and 5 self-extinguished hot flames continued as cool flames. Pressure, fuel flow and test day are not matched, so the contrast cannot be attributed to oxygen alone, and neither band includes 30% O2.

• Diluents (FLEX, linear model of burning rate on O2 fraction, pressure, droplet size, CO2 and He fractions). At fixed O2 fraction, replacing nitrogen with helium was associated with about +10% per 0.1 mole fraction and carbon dioxide with −2% to −5%, relative to the mean rate. This is an association within the tested range, not a general ranking of suppressants.

• Beyond the PSI tables, NASA reports hold solid-material tests near the Moon Base atmosphere. Saffire V and VI burned cotton jersey, SIBAL fabric and PMMA on Cygnus at 26.2–31% O2 and 54.1–70.7 kPa. The same 50 cm SIBAL sample burned for 112 s at 31% O2 (16.8 kPa O2) and 130 s at 22% O2 (22.0 kPa O2), a burn-duration ratio from one test each, not a measured spread rate. The CO2 increases in both PMMA tests exceed the cited 1-hour limit and three of five CO increases exceed the 24-hour limit; exposure depends on volume, mixing and scrubbing. In test VI-3 the far-field smoke reached the report's example 1 mg/m3 alarm threshold at 981 s on the test timeline (NTRS 20240002981). In a 5.18 s drop tower, flames survived at O2 levels 2.4–3.8 points below the 1-g upward limits; the report notes some might extinguish given longer time, so the definitions differ (NTRS 20080034883). Under the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, 30% O2 at 10.2 psia exceeds the maximum self-extinguishing O2 of 3 of 7 materials, against 1 of 7 at sea-level air; these are 1-g thresholds, not burn probabilities on the Moon (NTRS 20160001047). Values are transcribed from the report tables and checked against the page images.

Benefits. Users can compare reported conditions across experiments, inspect missing dimensions and trace each result to a source row or passage. The app supports evidence discovery and preparation for later modelling; it does not certify fire safety or supply absent experimental outcomes.

Remaining work. Six catalog investigations still have no loaded table. Some loaded tables contain conditions without result labels; solid-table pressure and partial-gravity validation remain unavailable. Further prediction work requires suitable labelled outcomes and validated physical models.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Zod, Node.js, csv-parse, unpdf, Oxlint and Prettier; the Anthropic Claude API (claude-opus-5-5) for SI answers, generated offline on request and cached. The public demo is a static build served from GitHub Pages (https://michaelwei08.github.io/flamemap/) and makes no model calls.
